notes.meaning: Naaman was the top general of the Syrian army and stood in high favor with his king. The Bible points out that the LORD, the true God of Israel, was the one who had given Syria its victories through him. Yet despite his wealth, bravery, and fame, Naaman suffered from leprosy, a painful and disfiguring skin disease. No amount of worldly honor can shield a person from the painful troubles of life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars note that the ancient Hebrew word for leprosy covered several severe skin disorders and rashes, not only the specific medical condition known today as Hansen's disease.

notes.meaning: Syrian raiders had invaded Israelite territory and captured a young Hebrew girl. She was brought into Syria and assigned to serve Naaman's wife. Even in the middle of this sad captivity, God placed her right where she could bring the message of His power.

The young servant girl kindly told her mistress that if Naaman visited the prophet living in Samaria, he would be cured of his leprosy. She did not hold bitterness against the family holding her captive, but wanted her master to be well. Her faith was strong, trusting that the prophet of the true God could do what no doctor could do.

Naaman went straight to his master, the king of Syria, and reported what the captive girl had said. He did not dismiss her words just because she was a young slave. When people are in deep pain and need, they are often willing to listen to the truth from anyone.

The king of Syria urged Naaman to go immediately and wrote an official letter for him to carry to the king of Israel. Naaman also took an enormous treasure of silver, gold, and fine garments to pay for his cure. He still assumed that God's great help could be bought like any earthly service.

Naaman delivered the letter to the king of Israel, asking him to cure the Syrian general of his leprosy. The Syrian king thought Israel's king could simply command a prophet to perform a miracle. This confusion set up an alarming misunderstanding between the two rulers.

When the king of Israel read the demand, he tore his robes in panic and grief, suspecting the Syrian king was looking for an excuse to start a war. He knew that only God has the power to bring life out of death and heal incurable leprosy. Because the king lacked real faith, he forgot that God had a prophet living right in his own land.

When Elisha heard that the king had torn his clothes, he sent a message telling him to stop worrying and send Naaman over. Elisha promised that Naaman would learn that the true God still had a real prophet in Israel. The prophet cared about clearing up the king's fear and showing God's power to the nations.

Naaman arrived at Elisha's modest house with his impressive horses and royal chariots. He halted at the entrance, expecting a grand greeting suited to his rank. God often humbles human pride by showing that His spiritual power does not depend on outward displays.

Instead of coming outside himself, Elisha sent a messenger to tell Naaman to wash seven times in the Jordan River. Doing this would fully heal his diseased skin and make him clean. The river water had no special medicine; it was a simple test of whether Naaman would humbly obey God's word.

Naaman left in a furious temper because Elisha did not even step out to meet him. He had pictured the prophet coming out, calling on the name of the LORD, and waving his hand over the sores in a dramatic ceremony. Pride often makes people angry when God does not work the way they expect.

Naaman argued that the sparkling mountain rivers of Damascus, the Abanah and Pharpar, were far cleaner and better than the muddy Jordan. He felt insulted by the simple command and stormed off in a rage. He failed to see that the healing would come from God's power, not the purity of the water.

Naaman's servants approached him with great gentleness and respect, calling him 'my father.' They wisely asked whether he would have gladly done some hard or heroic task if the prophet had demanded it. Since the prophet gave such an easy instruction, they begged him to just wash and be clean.

Naaman listened to his servants, went down into the Jordan valley, and dipped himself seven times as Elisha had said. When he came up the seventh time, his damaged skin was completely restored, as fresh and healthy as a little child's. God blesses those who put away their pride and follow His instructions in simple faith.

Naaman and his entire company returned to Elisha's home, and this time Naaman went inside to stand before the prophet. He boldly stated his new belief that there is no true God anywhere on earth except the God of Israel. Filled with gratitude, he urged Elisha to accept a rich present.

Elisha swore by the living God that he would not take a single thing, even when Naaman repeatedly urged him. The prophet wanted everyone to see that God's grace and healing are free gifts that cannot be bought. Refusing the payment protected God's honor and proved the prophet was not working for money.

Since Elisha would not take a gift, Naaman asked for as much dirt as two mules could carry back to Syria. He promised that he would never again sacrifice to any idol, but only to the LORD. As a brand-new believer, he felt he needed soil from Israel's holy land to build a proper altar for the true God.

Naaman asked the LORD to pardon him for one difficult duty: when his royal master went into the temple of the Syrian god Rimmon, the king leaned on Naaman's arm, forcing Naaman to bow along with him. Naaman wanted the prophet to know that his heart was not worshiping the idol, even if his court job made him bend his body. He was already feeling the tension between his new faith and his old life.

differ.view: Some read Naaman's words as asking pardon for his past idolatry before his healing, rather than asking permission to keep bowing in the idol temple in the future.

notes.meaning: Elisha gave Naaman a peaceful parting blessing, 'Go in peace,' rather than piling heavy rules on the new believer. The prophet trusted God to guide and teach Naaman as he grew in his new faith. Naaman then left and traveled a short distance down the road.

Elisha's servant Gehazi became filled with greed when he realized all that wealth had walked away untouched. He thought his master had been foolish to let a Syrian foreigner off without paying. Gehazi even used God's name in an oath as he planned to chase down Naaman and take a share for himself.

Gehazi hurried down the road until he caught up with Naaman's traveling party. When Naaman noticed him running, he stepped down from his chariot out of deep respect for Elisha. He greeted Gehazi with warmth and asked if anything had gone wrong.

Gehazi made up a clever lie, claiming that two poor young prophets had just arrived at Elisha's house needing help. He asked for a talent of silver and two sets of clothes in his master's name. He used a fake story of charity to cover his own selfish greed.

Naaman was glad to help and urged Gehazi to take double the silver he had requested. He packed two talents of silver into two bags along with the clothing and assigned two of his own servants to carry the heavy load. Naaman's grateful generosity stood in stark contrast to Gehazi's dishonest heart.

When they reached the hill near town, Gehazi took the bags from Naaman's men and hid the treasure safely inside his house. He then dismissed the Syrian servants so no one would find out what he had done. He thought his secret crime was completely hidden from view.

Gehazi walked back in and stood before Elisha as if he had been attending to ordinary chores the whole time. When Elisha asked where he had been, Gehazi flatly lied and said he had not gone anywhere. One sin almost always leads to another when someone tries to cover up their tracks.

Elisha revealed that God had shown him in spirit the moment Naaman stepped down from his chariot to greet Gehazi. He asked Gehazi if this was really the right time to seek riches, land, animals, and servants. Gehazi had shamed the Lord's name by turning a free miracle of grace into a chance to make money.

Elisha announced God's sentence: because Gehazi took Naaman's treasure, he and his family line would inherit Naaman's leprosy. The moment Gehazi turned to leave, his skin was struck with the disease, turning as white as snow. Trying to get rich through lies and greed brings God's judgment instead of true gain.
